analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set a legal limit for perchlorate rocket-fuel chemical in drinking water.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action; it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Perchlorate, a chemical used in rocket fuel and fireworks, has contaminated drinking water supplies, especially near military bases and aerospace plants. The bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to officially classify perchlorate as a contaminant and required the EPA to set a legal drinking water limit by July 1, 2004, with an extra margin of safety for children and pregnant women. It was introduced by Senator Barbara Boxer, sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water contaminated with perchlorate — particularly children and pregnant women, since the chemical can interfere with the thyroid and affect brain development. Residents near military installations and aerospace facilities in places like California would have gained a legally enforceable limit on the chemical in their tap water.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares perchlorate a contaminant under the Safe Drinking Water Act and requires the EPA to regulate it as an inorganic contaminant [S3].

It sets a firm deadline — July 1, 2004 — for the EPA to establish a maximum contaminant level that provides an adequate margin of safety for vulnerable populations, including children and pregnant women [S3] [S2].
A federal drinking water limit would give residents of affected communities an enforceable standard, rather than leaving perchlorate levels to ad hoc state decisions.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on the defense and aerospace operations and chemical makers responsible for perchlorate releases, who would face cleanup liability, and on water utilities that would have to test for and treat the chemical — costs partly passed to water ratepayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Defense contractors, chemical makers, water utilities

drawbacks.text: Water utilities would bear testing and treatment costs, and some of that cost would likely show up in water bills, including for households whose water was not contaminated.

The July 1, 2004 deadline left the EPA just over a year to set the standard, which a good-faith critic could call too fast for a rule normally built on years of health and treatment studies; a rushed limit risked being legally challenged or set at the wrong level.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — an enforceable, health-protective limit on a chemical that affects thyroid function in children and pregnant women — is substantial for the millions of people whose water is affected. The costs are real but ordinary for any drinking water standard: monitoring, treatment, and cleanup. The tight one-year deadline was the weakest design feature. On balance the public health benefit outweighed the compliance cost, which is what makes the bill's quiet death notable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and no committee ever acted on it; the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced S. 502 on March 3, 2003 [S5] [S1].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — its only action beyond introduction [S5].
The bill's entire action history consists of introduction and referral; there was no hearing, markup, floor vote, or House action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense and aerospace operations responsible for perchlorate contamination, along with chemical manufacturers, were better off because no enforceable federal drinking water limit was created, and water utilities avoided new treatment mandates. Communities with perchlorate in their water gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require an EPA drinking water limit for perchlorate and delivered introductory remarks; had no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. James Inhofe (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no Republican or Democrat joined as a cosponsor, and a Republican-led committee took no action; the record shows no cross-party support [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Defense and aerospace contractors (rocket propellant users)
industries.note: Perchlorate is a key ingredient in rocket and missile propellant, and releases from military and contractor sites are a major source of drinking water contamination. A federal maximum contaminant level would create enforceable cleanup and liability exposure they did not face while no standard existed.

An official designation of perchlorate as a regulated drinking water contaminant would increase scrutiny and cost for producers of the chemical. Their interest in avoiding a strict limit runs against the health interest of people drinking contaminated water.

Utilities would face new monitoring and treatment obligations and could pass costs to ratepayers, but a clear federal standard also ends uncertainty and shields utilities that comply. The burden is real but routine for any drinking water rule.
